chapter: Touring, recording and Fletcher's band in the 1940s
title: Sitting in with Fletcher's band before the army
summary: Horace regularly helped Fletcher at the Grand Terrace when his own job closed; Fletcher also wrote for Basie. Israel Crosby went from Horace's band to Fletcher's, and Fletcher often directed without a pianist.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: That's great. Okay. Apparently, right before you went in the army, which was November of '42, then you played with Fletcher's band again. Tell me about that. How did it really work, if you want to say? LIke if

you came to a point where, for one reason or another, you didn't have a job or your band had, you know, stopped a gig or something, did you often automatically go to Fletcher's band, or how did that work out?

Well, we always, as you know, were in constant contact with each other, being in the same city. Fletcher during that time used to exchange arrangements -- write arrangements -- even for Basie, you know, Basie had his great Kansas City band during that time. He had Buck Clayton in that band and Harry Sweets Edison, and Basie was making his little tours up through there, and he would come in and stop at the same hotel right down where Fletcher was playing at the Grand Terrace, you know. And a lot of times, Fletcher would be broadcasting, and it was pretty difficult to broadcast (unintelligible) and direct and play too. And I knew this, and he said whenever you -- you know, 'If you ever take off, you know, close your job, or and you're gonna have a few weeks off, why don't you come in and help out,' you know, one of these things. And I was always there, you know, because I wanted to get all the playin' time and experience in that I wanted. Of course, being around these great guys like Roy And Choo -- in fact, one time when the job closed, the band was out of work for quite a few months. And this is when Crosby went over to Fletcher from my band. Israel Crosby, the bassist.

So this is -- and then I went along too, and of course Fletcher liked that. He wasn't lazy or anything like that, but he knew he had to do a lot of writing and a lot of playing, and it was a difficult thing. Man, you know with a big band. It wasn't like a four piece combo, you know, where you can get by with sketches, you know, so this is what transpired.
What did he do during the times that you weren't -- did he just do without having extra hand there?
Yes. A lot of times I've even come in where he was playing, and he was just standing up sometimes through the whole arrangement directing.

Without the piano, and of course, if there was an important thing where the piano had to play chimes, or bells, or make modulations, he'd do that and jump right back up from the piano. And he had a guitarist with him that was an excellent guitarist -- John Collins. Do you remember that name? He was a legend, and he's still in New York, and he had another guitarist that -- I just scrapped a 'Down Beat' here the other day -- his name is Lawrence Lucey, and he has a music studio and he's teaching chords and all that stuff now. Well, he was with Fletcher's band during that time. But even having the guitar, it wasn't like -- you still had to play the piano, you know. And it helped the bass a lot too, you know, in those
days, you know, the string bass. But it was missed, but he had to do it, and I knew this, and it kept him busy.
